At 11 p.m. the class group was still buzzing about the fight. Wasim put his phone face down, then picked it up again and opened a private chat with Payal.

"That got out of hand. I don't want to do this in front of 40 people. Can we talk tomorrow before assembly, just us?"

Three dots. Gone. Three dots again. "ok. by the cycle stand."

Next morning Payal was already there, arms crossed.

"I thought you'd bring your whole gang," she said.

"No gang. Just me."

"You made me look stupid in the group."

"I know. And you called me a show-off in front of everyone."

"Yeah." She kicked at the gravel. "It's easier to be angry when everyone's watching."

"It's easier to talk when they're not."

Payal almost smiled. "So talk."

qa.q: Where did Wasim and Payal agree to meet?
qa.a: They agreed to meet by the cycle stand before assembly.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he picked the phone up again at 11 p.m.?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and tired of the public fight, wanting to fix things privately rather than keep performing for the group.

qa.q: Why did moving the talk to the cycle stand help?
qa.a: Without an audience there was no reputation to defend, so both could admit what hurt instead of scoring points.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt when Wasim came alone?
qa.a: Payal was probably surprised and a little relieved, expecting his friends and finding a real chance to talk.

grounding: One person sends a brief private message and meets face to face away from the group, which takes much of the heat out of the argument.

subtype: Stage 6: Owning your part, not the whole [Response]
passage:
The whole of 10-B had been split for a week over Saurabh and Sudha's fight about the science fair model. Today, in the corridor outside the chemistry lab, Saurabh stopped her.

"I'm sorry I said you did nothing on the model," he said quickly, before he could change his mind. "You did the wiring. That was the hard part. I said it because I was annoyed."

Sudha stared. She'd been ready for round two.

"I'm sorry I told everyone you were bossy," she said. "I shouldn't have gone round the class with it."

Neither of them said "but you started it." Neither asked the other to go first.

At lunch, Sudha sat at her usual place next to Saurabh's table. Within two days, the two "sides" in 10-B had quietly forgotten they were sides.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh stop Sudha?
qa.a: He stopped her in the corridor outside the chemistry lab.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when Saurabh apologised?
qa.a: She was surprised, having been ready for another round, and then felt able to own her part too.

qa.q: What made this repair work so well?
qa.a: Each named what they regretted without asking the other to apologise first, which put the friendship above who started it.

qa.q: How are the other students in 10-B affected by the repair?
qa.a: Once the two of them calmed down, the class stopped acting like two sides and the tension faded.

grounding: Two teens each own their part without demanding the other go first, and the whole class cools as they do.

subtype: Stage 1: Spark over a small thing [Actor]
passage:
The graduate residence at the university had four students to a kitchen, and on the third morning Madhuri opened the door to the same tower of plates in the sink.

Curry pan. Two mugs with tea rings. A plate with dried ketchup that she was fairly sure was Irfan's, since he'd made fries on Sunday.

Irfan wandered in, yawning.

"Oh good, the dishwasher's arrived," Madhuri said, not quite under her breath. "Do they teach washing up in your PhD, or is that beneath you?"

He blinked. "Morning to you too."

She slammed a cupboard harder than she meant to. It wasn't really the ketchup. It was the way her labelled milk kept vanishing, the way her notes on the fridge got moved, the way nobody seemed to notice she was the only one who ever cleaned. It had been building for weeks.

qa.q: How many students shared the kitchen?
qa.a: Four students shared a kitchen.

qa.q: What was Madhuri really upset about underneath the sarcasm?
qa.a: She felt unrespected and unseen, since her milk vanished, her notes were moved and nobody noticed that she did all the cleaning.

qa.q: What could Madhuri say instead of the sarcastic remark?
qa.a: She could tell Irfan and the others calmly that she feels she does most of the cleaning and ask to agree a plan together.

qa.q: How might Irfan see the moment?
qa.a: Irfan probably felt ambushed by a sharp comment first thing in the morning, without knowing the weeks of frustration behind it.

grounding: In a shared residence, a flatmate mutters sarcasm over dishes piled for days, while the real issue is a slowly building sense of disrespect.

passage:
The two rooms above the grocery shop in Sirsa were cheap, and Vijay and Amandeep had shared them since the start of their ITI course.

Amandeep came back from the tap with a scowl. "The water drum's empty again, Vijay. You never fill it."

Vijay felt the words land like an accusation in court. "Never? I filled it Monday. And Wednesday. Who swept the stairs on Sunday? Who paid the milkman when you forgot? Who fixed the fan?"

"I'm just saying the drum—"

"You're saying I'm lazy." Vijay's voice climbed. "I cook four nights out of seven. You want a list? I'll write you a list."

Amandeep went quiet. He had only wanted someone to fill the drum. Now he was somehow on trial, and so was Vijay, and neither of them had touched the drum.

qa.q: Where were the two rooms?
qa.a: They were above the grocery shop in Sirsa.

qa.q: Why did Vijay reply with a list of everything he had done?
qa.a: He heard Amandeep's complaint as an attack on his character and felt defensive, needing to prove he wasn't lazy.

qa.q: What could Vijay try next time a complaint feels like an attack?
qa.a: He could first ask what Amandeep actually needs, like a turn system for the drum, before defending himself.

qa.q: How is Amandeep affected by Vijay's reply?
qa.a: Amandeep is taken aback, having only wanted the drum filled, and now feels caught in an argument about who is the better flatmate.

grounding: A flatmate hears a complaint as an attack on his character and answers with a list of his contributions, turning a request into a trial.

passage:
By ten at night in their Andheri flat, Darshan and Harish weren't talking about the electricity bill anymore.

"You just don't care about anything in this flat," Darshan said. "You don't care about me, you don't care about the bills."

"And you think you're better than us because your job pays more," Harish shot back. "Don't pretend you don't."

"I never said that!"

"You didn't have to. It's how you look at my room."

Darshan laughed, a bitter sound. "See, now you're reading my mind. That's convenient."

"Oh, so now I'm lying?"

Darshan had never thought about Harish's room at all. Harish had once, honestly, forgotten the bill by accident. But neither of them could hear the other's denial now. Every "I didn't mean that" sounded like one more lie.

qa.q: Where did Darshan and Harish live?
qa.a: They lived in a flat in Andheri.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling behind that bitter laugh?
qa.a: Darshan felt frustrated and misjudged, accused of thoughts never actually held, and the anger hardened.

qa.q: What could either of them do to break this pattern?
qa.a: One of them could stop guessing motives and say only what happened and how it felt, or suggest a pause before talking again.

qa.q: How does Harish see Darshan at this point?
qa.a: Harish sees Darshan as looking down on Harish and treats that guess as fact, so any denial sounds false.

grounding: Two flatmates move to 'you just don't care' and 'you think you're better than us', treating guessed motives as fact so denials sound like lies.

subtype: Stage 4: Peak and point of no return [Actor]
passage:
The rented room in Sagar had one fan, two cots and a fight that had lasted since dinner.

Abhinav and his cousin Jyoti were preparing for the same state exam. She had cleared the prelims; he hadn't.

"At least I'm not wasting Chacha's money on a second attempt," Jyoti said.

The room went silent. Abhinav's father had taken a loan to send him here; everyone in the family knew.

Abhinav's face burned. "And at least my father didn't lose his shop because he trusted the wrong people," he said.

Jyoti flinched as if he'd slapped her. Her father's shop was the one thing nobody mentioned.

They stared at each other. Abhinav felt sick. He knew it was too far. So did she. But the words "I'm sorry" sat like stones in both their throats, and pride kept them there. Jyoti turned off the light without a word.

qa.q: What exam were Abhinav and Jyoti preparing for?
qa.a: They were preparing for the same state exam.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling right after his remark about the shop?
qa.a: He felt a flash of anger followed by shame and sickness, knowing it had gone too far, yet pride stopped his apology.

qa.q: What turning point is still available tonight or tomorrow?
qa.a: Either could break the silence with a short 'I shouldn't have said that about your father,' or ask for a pause and talk calmly in the morning.

qa.q: How might Jyoti be feeling as she turns off the light?
qa.a: Jyoti is likely hurt and ashamed of her own words too, but too proud and wounded to speak first.

grounding: In a small-town rented room, two cousins land cruel remarks on known sore spots, both feeling shame and anger while pride blocks taking it back.

passage:
I'm Rustom, the third person in this flat, so I was on the sofa when Wasim and Manoj really went at it about the rent split.

Voices up. Manoj said something about Wasim's "rich-boy habits." Wasim stood, red in the face, and I thought he was about to slam out like last time.

Instead he said, "I'm too angry to talk properly. Can we continue at nine? I'll be back." And he picked up his keys and left, closing the door normally.

Manoj just sat there. I could tell he didn't know what to do with it. Last time Wasim walked out, Manoj didn't sleep.

At 8:55 the lock turned. Wasim came in, put two chais on the table and said, "Okay. Let's try again."

I went to my room. Through the wall, I heard them talking, not shouting.

qa.q: What time did Wasim say they would continue?
qa.a: He said they would continue at nine.

qa.q: What might Wasim have been feeling when he stood up red in the face?
qa.a: He was probably very angry and hurt by the rich-boy remark, but he chose to pause rather than lash out or storm off.

qa.q: Why did Wasim's pause work better than walking out?
qa.a: He named the reason, gave a return time and came back on time, so Manoj could wait without feeling punished.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt while waiting for Wasim to come back?
qa.a: Manoj was probably unsettled and unsure, remembering the last walk-out, and likely relieved when Wasim returned with chai.

grounding: An observer watches one flatmate call a time-out with a return time and actually come back, unlike storming off.

subtype: Stage 6: Repair and one concrete agreement [Response]
passage:
Sumit,

Writing this down after our talk so we both remember it.

You said you feel like you're the only one who notices when the bathroom's dirty, and that when I said "chill, it's fine," it felt like I was calling you fussy. Did I get that right?

My side: I've felt nagged, like every time you walk in you're checking. But I also said you were "worse than my mother," and that was a cheap shot. I'm sorry for that one specifically.

You owned calling me lazy in front of Anmol. Thank you. That stung more than the rest.

So, what we agreed: bathroom on a two-week rota, taped on the door. Your weeks are odd, mine even. If one of us misses, we swap, no speeches.

That's it. I feel lighter. Hope you do too.

Jasleen

qa.q: How often does the bathroom rota switch?
qa.a: The bathroom is on a two-week rota.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's letter suggest about how Jasleen feels after the talk?
qa.a: Jasleen feels lighter and relieved, with some lingering hurt from being called lazy in front of Anmol.

qa.q: Why is the rota a good way to end the argument?
qa.a: A clear practical plan with a rule for misses holds up better than good feelings alone, giving them less to fight about.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sumit may feel understood, since Jasleen restated Sumit's point first and apologised for the specific cheap shot.

grounding: A written summary shows two flatmates restating each other's point, owning their harshest words and leaving with a simple rota.

passage:
Counselling centre, student session note, Tuesday.

Darshan, a second-year student, came in saying he "just needed to vent." Over forty minutes, a pattern emerged. His girlfriend, Indu, has been busy with her theatre rehearsals for six weeks, and they talk less.

He described checking when she was last online, sending "Everything okay with us?" at midnight, and hinting that "some people make time." He said his tone has been sharper than he intends. When asked what he was most afraid of, he was quiet, then said, "That she'll get bored of me and I'll be the last to know."

I noted the fear of being left sitting under the questions and hints. Next step agreed: before our next session, he will try one direct, calm sentence to Indu about what he misses, instead of a hint. We'll look at how it went on Friday.

qa.q: How long has Indu been busy with theatre rehearsals?
qa.a: She has been busy for six weeks.

qa.q: What is Darshan most afraid of?
qa.a: He is afraid Indu will get bored of him and leave, and that he will be the last to know.

qa.q: Why is one calm, direct sentence a useful next step?
qa.a: It lets Darshan ask for what he really needs, closeness and reassurance, without the hints and sharp tone that could push Indu away.

qa.q: How might Indu be experiencing Darshan's midnight messages?
qa.a: Indu may feel pressured or confused by the hints and sharp tone, unaware of the fear of being left that lies under them.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young man craving reassurance, with fear of being left coming out as questions, hints and a sharper tone.

The bus was forty minutes late, the rain was sideways, and Afreen had already sent Devesh six messages by the time she reached their rented flat in Indore.

"u home?"
"can we talk tonight"
"like properly"
"??"
"you've been so distant"
"I'm scared something's wrong with us"

No replies. The last one said "delivered" but not "read."

She was still dripping in the hallway when his key turned. Devesh stepped in, soaked and grey from his double shift.

"What is wrong with us?" she said before he'd even taken his shoes off. "Why won't you talk to me?"

He stood very still, one shoe on. She could see him shrinking, but she only felt more certain: if they just talked now, all of it, he'd come back to her. She stepped closer.

qa.q: How many messages had Afreen sent Devesh?
qa.a: She had sent him six messages.

qa.q: Why does Afreen push for a talk the moment Devesh walks in?
qa.a: She is scared of losing closeness and believes a big talk right now is the only way to reach him.

qa.q: What could Afreen try instead, given Devesh has just come off a double shift?
qa.a: She could say she's been feeling far from him and ask for a set time to talk once he's rested, which gives the talk a better chance.

qa.q: How might Devesh feel standing in the hallway with one shoe on?
qa.a: Devesh is exhausted and likely feels cornered and flooded, which makes him want to pull back rather than talk.

grounding: Under stress from rain and a late bus, a young woman sends many messages and presses for a talk the instant her partner walks in.
